COLM 2026 WORKSHOP ON EFFICIENT REASONING (ER) · ACCEPTED PAPER #171

50× COMPUTE SAVINGS

Before You Scale: The Cost of Supervision Mismatch in PRM Distillation

0.3h Diagnostic vs 15h Sweep
88.8% of No-GT gap is format

Saksham Kapoor*¹·² · Henry Tran¹·³ · Edward Lue Chee Lip¹·⁴ · Charlotte Le¹

OpenReview #171

*Presenter ¹Algoverse ²University of Maryland, College Park ³University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) ⁴Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University / CSU

01 BACKGROUND & METHODS PIPELINE

02 RESULTS (FIGURES & EMPIRICAL DATA)

• The Reflexive Scaling Trap: When small verifiers fail, researchers reflexively scale
student parameters (1.5B → 7B/70B) or sweep 15+ recipes. But when supervision is
format-mismatched, compute is wasted on an unlearnable target.
• Core Research Objective: Decouple supervision format mismatch from student
capacity. Provide a 50× cheaper diagnostic gate before running large-scale PRM
distillation sweeps.

Do this first — 4 steps, 50× cheaper:
• 1 · Probe cheap (0.3h): 500-step LoRA on 1× GPU, ~18 min.
• 2 · Check format: Do scores match test? (+1/−1, first-error).
• 3 · Re-render, don't relabel: Reformat same traces — recovers 88.8% No-GT gap*.
• 4 · Then scale: Scale to 7B/70B only if probe passes; else fix data first.
*5k sequence-cluster bootstrap paired gap; No-GT only.

CAPACITY PROBES (RULING OUT STUDENT MODEL SIZE):

• Teacher Paradox (MATH Sweet Spot): Privileged worked solutions improve
Gemma-4-26B error localization (+0.051 F1, 0.726 → 0.777, N=400), rescuing 33% of
self-verification failures on MATH. (+Answer alone yields 0 delta; rich traces required!)
• The Distillation Null: Distilled into 1.5B, privilege gives 0 edge (ROC-AUC 0.631 vs
0.641; downstream BoN 0.349 vs 0.373, lagging majority vote 0.391). Why? 31%
disagreement has 50/50 symmetric churn (1,001 vs 956 steps)!

• MATH 200/200 Score-Head: Reaches 0.7129 ROC-AUC when trained & evaluated on matched
data.
• Frozen Representation Probe: Reaches 0.6308 ROC-AUC on gold labels without fine-tuning.
→ 3B student can learn verification; failure is primarily supervision mismatch!

• Scope: Math step-level error localization only; OlympiadBench n=2 high-variance; first-error vs

• Core Conclusion: Format matching precedes parameter scaling. Re-rendering recovers the
majority of lost signal without new rollouts.
• Future Directions: Automated cross-schema alignment pipelines and universal multi-task
reward verifier distillation.

Under review as a conference paper at COLM 2026

Before You Scale: The Cost of Supervision Mismatch in PRM
Distillation
Anonymous authors
Paper under double-blind review

Abstract
Process reward models (PRMs) are commonly trained from automatically
generated step-level supervision, but when a small verifier fails it is often
unclear whether the bottleneck is student capacity, the training recipe, or the
supervision itself. This distinction matters for efficient reasoning systems:
if supervision distribution is the bottleneck, then scaling student compute
or searching over nearby training recipes can be inefficient until the data
problem is addressed. We study this question under a fixed student and
evaluation path that holds the architecture, optimization path, and benchmark constant while varying the source, annotation provenance, and format
of process supervision. Using the same Qwen2.5-3B score-head verifier and
full ProcessBench-MATH evaluation, ProcessBench-style labels from nonMATH source splits transfer reliably to MATH: GSM8K-source supervision
reaches 0.7515 mean ROC-AUC over four seeds, and OmniMath-source
supervision reaches 0.7694. OlympiadBench-source supervision is highvariance, spanning 0.585–0.716, showing that format match alone is not
sufficient. In contrast, generated teacher-label supervision is markedly
weaker under the same evaluation path: a four-seed generated no-GT rankloss baseline reaches 0.6062 mean ROC-AUC. We further show that this
failure is primarily driven by rendering convention: simply re-rendering
the generated labels into the ProcessBench format closes much of the gap,
raising the generated no-GT baseline to 0.7366 mean ROC-AUC. The practical conclusion for efficient PRM development is that a cheap source- and
format-matched diagnostic can reveal supervision mismatch before investing in larger students or broader recipe searches.

Introduction

Process reward models assign scores to intermediate reasoning steps and are increasingly
used to supervise or verify mathematical reasoning systems (1; 3). Because human step-level
annotation is expensive, many PRM pipelines rely on automatically generated labels from
stronger models. This raises a practical question for efficient reasoning systems: when
a distilled verifier performs poorly, should we scale the student and training budget, or
should we first question whether the generated supervision matches the target evaluation
distribution? If supervision distribution is the primary bottleneck, then scaling student
compute or searching over nearby training recipes can be inefficient until the data problem
is addressed.
We investigate this question with a fixed-path diagnostic ablation. We fix the verifier
architecture, training path, and evaluation benchmark, and vary the source, annotation
provenance, and format of step-level supervision. The student is a Qwen2.5-3B model with
a lightweight score head. The target benchmark is full ProcessBench-MATH, evaluated
over 1,000 shuffled solutions containing 6,505 reasoning steps and 594 error steps (2). We
compare ProcessBench-style supervision from non-MATH source splits against generated
teacher labels from a privileged/no-ground-truth labeling pipeline.
The same 3B verifier that learns a transferable ProcessBench-MATH scorer from GSM8K or
OmniMath ProcessBench-style labels remains weak when trained on generated teacher labels. This contrast is not a state-of-the-art PRM claim: a public Qwen2.5-Math-7B-PRM800K

Large Language Models display skin tone biases in the evaluation of common dermatological conditions
Kiran Nijjer1, Benjamin Liu2, Derek Jiu2, Adnan Ahmed2, Peter Wang2, Ryan Bui2, Kevin Zhu2, Lilly Zhu MD3
1
Stanford University Department of Computer Science; 2Algoverse; 3Brentwood Dermatology

Background

Results

● SkinGPT-4, a large vision-language model, leverages datasets of annotated skin
disease images to augment clinical workflows and treatments in underserved
communities.
● Existing training dataset predominantly represents lighter skin tones, and may limit
diagnostic accuracy for darker skin tones.
● We evaluated performance biases in SkinGPT-4 across skin tones on common skin
diseases, including eczema, allergic-contact dermatitis, and psoriasis on the open
sourced SCIN dataset.

Fig 2. SkinGPT-4 Performance Metrics Across Fitzpatrick Skin Tones

Objectives/Aims
● Evaluate SkinGPT-4’s diagnostic accuracy and fairness across skin tones,
identifying biases in common dermatological conditions.
● Evaluate SkinGPT-4’s clinical applicability and diagnostic potential, examining
its analytical accuracy, usability for the general public, and overall effectiveness
beyond bias detection.

Limitations

● Limitations include potential biases and limited representation of diverse skin
tones in the dataset.
● Reliance on subjective assessments by dermatologists.
● Possibility of model hallucinations affecting diagnostic accuracy.
● Dermatologists evaluated an outdated Llama version of SkinGPT, not the latest
model, potentially affecting performance assessment.
● SkinGPT provides only one diagnosis, which may lower clinical evaluation
performance since skin disease diagnosis is more complex than a single
classification.
●

Conclusions
● SkinGPT-4 demonstrates weaker performances on darker skin tones compared
to lighter skin tones among prevalent skin conditions.
● Model biases exist across diverse evaluation criteria, and model hallucinations
may affect diagnostic efficacy.
● Further research is needed to better understand and mitigate biases in large
vision-language models to promote equitable deployment in dermatological
workflows.

Future Directions
Methods

● Integrate modules to detect and minimize model hallucinations, particularly
regarding anatomical or physical inaccuracies.
● Gather additional feedback and insights from a wider range of dermatologists to
ensure diverse perspectives and enhance the model's clinical relevance and
accuracy.
● Evaluate the model on a broader range of diseases to identify trends in
performance.
● Extend the research to include clinical trials, testing SkinGPT-4 in real-world
patient settings to evaluate its effectiveness and reliability in diagnosing skin
conditions across different populations.
● Explore a broader range of LLM architectures beyond SkinGPT, since
SkinGPT's model architecture may not be the most optimal choice for skin
disease identification.

● A clinical evaluation of SkinGPT-4 was conducted by board-certified dermatologists
on six clinically relevant skin diseases, including eczema, allergic contact dermatitis,
impetigo, psoriasis, tinea and urticaria, from 300 cases in the open-sourced SCIN dataset.
● Images were assessed based on diagnostic accuracy, informativity, physician utility,
and patient utility.
● Model fairness metrics, including democratic parity and equalized odds, were
calculated over skin tones for each evaluated condition.

Before You Scale: The Cost of Supervision Mismatch
in PRM Distillation
Anonymous authors
Paper under double-blind review

Abstract
Process reward models (PRMs) are commonly trained from automatically
generated step-level supervision, but when a small verifier fails it is often
unclear whether the bottleneck is student capacity, the training recipe, or the
supervision itself. The distinction matters for efficient reasoning systems: if
supervision is the bottleneck, scaling student compute or searching over
nearby training recipes is wasted effort until the data problem is addressed.
We motivate the question with a concrete failure. Privileged (answer-aware)
labeling helps our teacher only in a tractability sweet spot (on MATH,
+0.051 first-error F1), yet a 1.5B student distilled from privileged labels
is statistically indistinguishable from one trained on answer-blind labels,
and a positive control shows the pipeline does track coarse teacher quality.
We then diagnose the failure under a fixed student and evaluation path,
varying only the source, provenance, and format of supervision. With the
same Qwen2.5-3B score-head verifier on full ProcessBench-MATH, gold
ProcessBench-style labels from non-MATH splits transfer reliably (GSM8Ksource 0.7515 mean ROC-AUC over four seeds; OmniMath-source 0.7694),
while OlympiadBench-source supervision is high-variance (0.585–0.716),
showing format match alone is not sufficient. Generated teacher labels are
markedly weaker under the same path (four-seed no-GT rank-loss baseline:
0.6062). The failure is primarily one of rendering convention: re-rendering
the same generated labels into the ProcessBench format raises the no-GT
baseline to 0.7366. The practical conclusion for efficient PRM development
is that a cheap source- and format-matched diagnostic, roughly 0.3 GPUhours against the ∼15 GPU-hours of the recipe sweep it replaces, can reveal
supervision mismatch before any compute is committed to larger students
or broader recipe searches.

Introduction

Process reward models assign scores to intermediate reasoning steps and are increasingly
used to supervise or verify mathematical reasoning systems (Lightman et al., 2023; Wang
et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025). Because human step-level annotation is expensive, many
PRM pipelines rely on automatically generated labels from stronger models. This raises a
practical question for efficient reasoning systems: when a distilled verifier performs poorly,
should we scale the student and training budget, or should we first question whether the
generated supervision matches the target evaluation distribution? If supervision distribution
is the primary bottleneck, then scaling student compute or searching over nearby training
recipes can be inefficient until the data problem is addressed.
We arrive at this question from a concrete failure. In our pipeline, a labeling teacher with
privileged (answer-aware) access to reference solutions produces measurably better steperror labels in a characterizable difficulty window (§3), yet a small student verifier distilled
from those labels is no better than one distilled from answer-blind labels (§4). A positive
control shows the training pipeline does transmit coarse teacher quality, so the null demands
a diagnosis rather than a shrug.

Large Language Models display skin tone biases in the evaluation of common dermatological conditions
Kiran Nijjer1, Benjamin Liu2, Derek Jiu2, Adnan Ahmed2, Peter Wang2, Ryan Bui2, Kevin Zhu2, Lilly Zhu MD3
1
Stanford University Department of Computer Science; 2Algoverse; 3Brentwood Dermatology

Background

Results

● SkinGPT-4, a large vision-language model, leverages datasets of annotated skin
disease images to augment clinical workflows and treatments in underserved
communities.
● Existing training dataset predominantly represents lighter skin tones, and may limit
diagnostic accuracy for darker skin tones.
● We evaluated performance biases in SkinGPT-4 across skin tones on common skin
diseases, including eczema, allergic-contact dermatitis, and psoriasis on the open
sourced SCIN dataset.

Objectives/Aims
● Evaluate SkinGPT-4’s diagnostic accuracy and fairness across skin tones,
identifying biases in common dermatological conditions.
● Evaluate SkinGPT-4’s clinical applicability and diagnostic potential, examining
its analytical accuracy, usability for the general public, and overall effectiveness
beyond bias detection.

● Limitations include potential biases and limited representation of diverse skin
tones in the dataset.
● Reliance on subjective assessments by dermatologists.
● Possibility of model hallucinations affecting diagnostic accuracy.
● Dermatologists evaluated an outdated Llama version of SkinGPT, not the latest
model, potentially affecting performance assessment.
● SkinGPT provides only one diagnosis, which may lower clinical evaluation
performance since skin disease diagnosis is more complex than a single
classification.
●

Conclusions
● SkinGPT-4 demonstrates weaker performances on darker skin tones compared
to lighter skin tones among prevalent skin conditions.
● Model biases exist across diverse evaluation criteria, and model hallucinations
may affect diagnostic efficacy.
● Further research is needed to better understand and mitigate biases in large
vision-language models to promote equitable deployment in dermatological
workflows.

Future Directions
Methods

● Integrate modules to detect and minimize model hallucinations, particularly
regarding anatomical or physical inaccuracies.
● Gather additional feedback and insights from a wider range of dermatologists to
ensure diverse perspectives and enhance the model's clinical relevance and
accuracy.
● Evaluate the model on a broader range of diseases to identify trends in
performance.
● Extend the research to include clinical trials, testing SkinGPT-4 in real-world
patient settings to evaluate its effectiveness and reliability in diagnosing skin
conditions across different populations.
● Explore a broader range of LLM architectures beyond SkinGPT, since
SkinGPT's model architecture may not be the most optimal choice for skin
disease identification.

● A clinical evaluation of SkinGPT-4 was conducted by board-certified dermatologists
on six clinically relevant skin diseases, including eczema, allergic contact dermatitis,
impetigo, psoriasis, tinea and urticaria, from 300 cases in the open-sourced SCIN dataset.
● Images were assessed based on diagnostic accuracy, informativity, physician utility,
and patient utility.
● Model fairness metrics, including democratic parity and equalized odds, were
calculated over skin tones for each evaluated condition.
